{{short description|Sumset of a field subject to a specific polynomial restriction}}
In [[additive number theory]] and [[additive combinatorics|combinatorics]], a '''restricted sumset''' has the form 

:<math>S=\{a_1+\cdots+a_n:\ a_1\in A_1,\ldots,a_n\in A_n \ \mathrm{and}\ P(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\not=0\},</math>

where <math> A_1,\ldots,A_n</math> are finite [[empty set|nonempty]] [[subset]]s of a [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''F'' and <math>P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is a [[polynomial]] over ''F''. 

If <math>P</math> is a constant non-zero function, for example <math>P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=1</math> for any <math>x_1,\ldots,x_n</math>, then <math>S</math> is the usual [[sumset]] <math>A_1+\cdots+A_n</math> which is denoted by <math>nA</math> if <math>A_1=\cdots=A_n=A.</math>

When 

:<math>P(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le n} (x_j-x_i),</math>

''S'' is written as <math>A_1\dotplus\cdots\dotplus A_n</math> which is denoted by <math>n^{\wedge} A</math> if <math>A_1=\cdots=A_n=A.</math>

Note that |''S''| > 0 if and only if there exist <math>a_1\in A_1,\ldots,a_n\in A_n</math> with <math>P(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\not=0.</math>

== Cauchy–Davenport theorem ==
The '''Cauchy–Davenport theorem''', named after [[Augustin Louis Cauchy]] and [[Harold Davenport]], asserts that for any [[prime number|prime]] ''p'' and nonempty subsets ''A'' and ''B'' of the prime-[[order of a group|order]] [[cyclic group]] <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> we have the [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]]<ref>Nathanson (1996) p.44</ref><ref name=GR1412>Geroldinger & Ruzsa (2009) pp.141–142</ref><ref>{{Cite arXiv|eprint = 1202.1816|author1 = Jeffrey Paul Wheeler|title = The Cauchy-Davenport Theorem for Finite Groups|year = 2012| class=math.CO }}</ref>

:<math>|A+B| \ge \min\{p,\, |A|+|B|-1\}</math>

where <math>A+B := \{a+b \pmod p \mid a \in A, b \in B\}</math>, i.e. using [[modular arithmetic]]. It can be generalised to arbitrary (not necessarily abelian) groups using a [[Dyson's transform|Dyson transform]]. If <math>A, B</math> are subsets of a group <math>G</math>, then<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeVos |first=Matt |date=2016 |title=On a Generalization of the Cauchy-Davenport Theorem |url=http://math.colgate.edu/~integers/q7/q7.Abstract.html |journal=Integers |volume=16}}</ref>

:<math>|AB| \ge \min\{p(G),\, |A|+|B|-1\}</math>

where <math>p(G)</math> is the size of the smallest nontrivial subgroup of <math>G</math> (we set it to <math>\infty</math> if there is no such subgroup).

This can be used to deduce the [[Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv theorem]]: given any sequence of 2''n''−1 elements in the cyclic group <math>\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}</math>, there are ''n'' elements that sum to zero modulo ''n''.  (Here ''n'' does not need to be prime.)<ref>Nathanson (1996) p.48</ref><ref name="GR53">Geroldinger & Ruzsa (2009) p.53</ref>

A direct consequence of the Cauchy-Davenport theorem is: Given any sequence ''S'' of ''p''−1 or more nonzero elements, not necessarily distinct, of <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math>, every element of <math>\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}</math> can be written as the sum of the elements of some [[subsequence]] (possibly empty) of ''S''.<ref>Wolfram's MathWorld, Cauchy-Davenport Theorem, http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Cauchy-DavenportTheorem.html, accessed 20 June 2012.</ref>

[[Kneser's theorem (combinatorics)|Kneser's theorem]] generalises this to general [[abelian group]]s.<ref name=GR143>Geroldinger & Ruzsa (2009) p.143</ref>

== Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture ==
The '''Erdős–Heilbronn conjecture''' posed by [[Paul Erdős]] and [[Hans Heilbronn]] in 1964 states that <math>|2^\wedge A| \ge \min\{p,\, 2|A|-3\}</math> if ''p'' is a prime and ''A'' is a nonempty subset of the field '''Z'''/''p'''''Z'''.<ref>Nathanson (1996) p.77</ref>  This was first confirmed by J. A. Dias da Silva and Y. O. Hamidoune in 1994<ref>{{cite journal
 |author1=Dias da Silva, J. A. |author2=Hamidoune, Y. O.
 | title = Cyclic spaces for Grassmann derivatives and additive theory
 | journal = [[London Mathematical Society|Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society]]
 | volume = 26
 | year = 1994
 | pages = 140–146
 | doi = 10.1112/blms/26.2.140
 | issue = 2}}</ref>
who showed that 

:<math>|n^\wedge A| \ge \min\{p(F),\ n|A|-n^2+1\},</math>

where ''A'' is a finite nonempty subset of a field ''F'', and ''p''(''F'') is a prime ''p'' if ''F'' is of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] ''p'', and ''p''(''F'') = ∞ if ''F'' is of characteristic 0. Various extensions of this result were given by [[Noga Alon]], M. B. Nathanson and [[Imre Z. Ruzsa|I. Ruzsa]] in 1996,<ref name="Alon1996"/> Q. H. Hou and [[Zhi-Wei Sun]] in 2002,<ref>{{cite journal
 |author1=Hou, Qing-Hu |author2-link=Zhi-Wei Sun
 |author2=Sun, Zhi-Wei
 | title = Restricted sums in a field
 | journal = [[Acta Arithmetica]]
 | volume = 102
 | year = 2002
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 239–249
 | mr = 1884717 
 | doi = 10.4064/aa102-3-3| bibcode = 2002AcAri.102..239H
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref>
and G. Karolyi in 2004.<ref>{{cite journal
 | author = Károlyi, Gyula
 | title = The Erdős–Heilbronn problem in abelian groups
 | journal = [[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]
 | volume = 139
 | year = 2004
 | pages = 349–359
 | mr = 2041798 
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02787556| s2cid = 33387005
 }}</ref>

== Combinatorial Nullstellensatz ==
A tool in the study of lower bounds for [[cardinalities]] of various restricted sumsets is the following principle: the combinatorial [[Nullstellensatz]].<ref name="Alon1999">{{cite journal
 | author = Alon, Noga
 | url = http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~nogaa/PDFS/null2.pdf
 | title = Combinatorial Nullstellensatz
 | journal = [[Combinatorics, Probability and Computing]]
 | volume = 8
 | issue = 1–2
 | year = 1999
 | pages = 7–29
 | mr = 1684621 
 | doi = 10.1017/S0963548398003411| s2cid = 209877602
 | author-link = Noga Alon
 }}</ref> Let <math>f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> be a polynomial over a field <math>F</math>.  Suppose that the [[coefficient]] of the [[monomial]] <math>x_1^{k_1}\cdots x_n^{k_n}</math> in <math>f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math> is nonzero and <math>k_1+\cdots+k_n</math> is the [[total degree]] of <math>f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)</math>. If <math>A_1,\ldots,A_n</math> are finite subsets of <math>F</math> with <math>|A_i|>k_i</math> for <math>i=1,\ldots,n</math>, then there are <math>a_1\in A_1,\ldots,a_n\in A_n</math> such that <math>f(a_1,\ldots,a_n) \neq 0</math>.

This result was rooted in a paper of [[Noga Alon|N. Alon]] and M. Tarsi in 1989,<ref>{{cite journal
 |author1=Alon, Noga |author2=Tarsi, Michael
 | title = A nowhere-zero point in linear mappings
 | journal = [[Combinatorica]]
 | volume = 9
 | year = 1989
 | pages = 393–395
 | mr = 1054015 
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02125351
 | issue = 4|s2cid=8208350
 |author1-link=Noga Alon
 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.163.2348
 }}</ref> 
and developed by Alon, Nathanson and Ruzsa in 1995–1996,<ref name="Alon1996">{{cite journal
 |author1=Alon, Noga |author2=Nathanson, Melvyn B. |author3=Ruzsa, Imre
 | url = http://www.math.tau.ac.il/~nogaa/PDFS/anrf3.pdf
 | title = The polynomial method and restricted sums of congruence classes
 | journal = [[Journal of Number Theory]]
 | volume = 56
 | issue = 2
 | year = 1996
 | pages = 404–417
 | mr = 1373563 
 | doi = 10.1006/jnth.1996.0029|author1-link=Noga Alon }}</ref> 
and reformulated by Alon in 1999.<ref name="Alon1999"/>
